MANAGING DROUGHT-VULNERABLE NATURAL RESOURCES IS A GROWING CHALLENGE FOR FEDERAL, STATE AND TRIBAL LAND MANAGERS. PLANT COMMUNITIES AND ANIMAL POPULATIONS ARE STRONGLY LINKED TO PATTERNS OF DROUGHT AND SOIL MOISTURE AVAILABILITY. AS A RESULT, ECOSYSTEMS MAY BE HEAVILY ALTERED BY FUTURE CHANGES IN PRECIPITATION AND SOIL MOISTURE THAT ARE DRIVEN BY CLIMATE CHANGE. ALTHOUGH THIS VULNERABILITY IS WELL RECOGNIZED, DEVELOPING ACCURATE INFORMATION ABOUT THE POTENTIAL CONSEQUENCES OF CLIMATE CHANGE FOR ECOLOGICAL DROUGHT IS DIFFICULT BECAUSE THE SOIL MOISTURE CONDITIONS THAT PLANTS EXPERIENCE ARE SHAPED BY COMPLEX INTERACTIONS AMONG WEATHER, ATMOSPHERIC CO2, PLANTS AND SOILS. THERE ARE CURRENTLY VERY FEW ECOLOGICALLY APPROPRIATE DATASETS ABOUT FUTURE DROUGHT WITH WIDESPREAD DISTRIBUTION AT RESOLUTIONS SUITABLE FOR INFORMING NATURAL RESOURCE DECISION MAKING. THIS PROJECT WILL MEET SOME OF THOSE NEEDS BY SIMULATING COMPLEX INTERACTIONS THAT AFFECT SOIL MOISTURE AVAILABILITY TO PLANTS AND GENERATING USER-RELEVANT SOIL MOISTURE PROJECTIONS FOR SCENARIO PLANNING AND ECOLOGICAL DROUGHT ASSESSMENT. PROJECT TITLE: SOUTHWEST CLIMATE ADAPTATION SCIENCE CENTERPROJECT DATES: 9 8 2024 THROUGH 9 7 2029AWARD PURPOSE: THOUGH PUNCTUATED BY OCCASIONAL FLOODS, SINCE 2000, THE U.S. SOUTHWEST HAS BEEN ENTRENCHED IN ONE OF THE WORST PROLONGED DROUGHTS IN OVER 1200 YEARS, WITH CLIMATE CHANGE LIMITING ABILITY TO MANAGE FRESHWATER, WILDLIFE, COASTAL EROSION, WILDFIRES, NATIVE PLANT SPECIES, AND CULTURAL RESOURCES. TICKS ARE ONE OF THE MOST IMPORTANT VECTORS OF DISEASE IN NORTH AMERICA  HOWEVER, THEIR PRESENCE IN DESERT ECOSYSTEMS IS OFTEN UNDERESTIMATED. IT IS NOT YET UNDERSTOOD WHY THIS TICK HAS RECENTLY APPEARED IN ARIZONA. PROJECT TITLE: CO-PRODUCTION FOR CLIMATE CHANGE ADAPTATION IN LODGEPOLE PINE FORESTS CRITICAL TO THE CASSIA CROSSBILL  IDAHOS ONLY ENDEMIC BIRD SPECIESDATES: 4 1 2026 TO 6 30 2029AWARD PURPOSE: THE CASSIA CROSSBILL, RECOGNIZED AS A DISTINCT SPECIES SINCE 2017, IS FOUND IN THE ALBION MOUNTAINS AND SOUTH HILLS OF SOUTHERN IDAHO. CROSSBILLS RELY ON LODGEPOLE PINE SEEDS, WHICH ARE PROTECTED IN CONES THAT  OTHER THAN WHEN FORCIBLY OPENED BY STRONG-BEAKED SPECIES LIKE CROSSBILLS AND WOODPECKERS  TYPICALLY OPEN ONLY DURING INTENSE HEAT SUCH AS DURING WILDFIRES. INCREASINGLY HOT AND DRY WEATHER THREATENS THIS FOOD SOURCE IN TWO WAYS: (1) INCREASED POTENTIAL FOR LARGE WILDFIRES THAT CAN REMOVE SUITABLE HABITAT FROM A SPECIFIC AREA FOR DECADES, AND (2) PREMATURE OPENING OF LODGEPOLE CONES WHEN EXPOSED TO ESPECIALLY HIGH TEMPERATURES.BECAUSE CASSIA CROSSBILLS ARE NOT KNOWN TO FEED ON SEEDS DROPPED FROM OPENED CONES, THEY RELY ON THE CANOPY SEED BANK STORED IN THESE CONES THAT REMAIN CLOSED. MORE FREQUENT HIGH-TEMPERATURE DAYS (OVER 90 DEGREES FAHRENHEIT) IN THESE FORESTS COULD SIGNIFICANTLY REDUCE THEIR FOOD SUPPLY, POTENTIALLY LEADING TO POPULATION DECLINES. IN RESPONSE, THE MINIDOKA RANGER DISTRICT OF THE SAWTOOTH NATIONAL FOREST  THE AGENCY RESPONSIBLE FOR HABITAT MANAGEMENT THROUGHOUT THE CASSIA CROSSBILL RANGE  HAS SHIFTED ITS MANAGEMENT FOCUS TO PRIORITIZE BOTH CASSIA CROSSBILLS AND LODGEPOLE PINE, ALONGSIDE OTHER KEY WILDLIFE HABITATS SUCH AS ASPEN. TO SUCCEED, THE SAWTOOTH NATIONAL FOREST AND PARTNER AGENCIES REQUIRE MORE INFORMATION ON CROSSBILL HABITAT NEEDS, AND MORE ANALYSIS PRODUCTS TO GUIDE THEIR SPECIFIC MANAGEMENT ACTIONS IN THE CONTEXT OF A CHANGING CLIMATE. THIS PROJECT AIMS TO BUILD ON THE EARLY MOMENTUM OF THE CASSIA CROSSBILL WORKING GROUP, FORMED IN 2021, TO PROVIDE THE SCIENTIFIC PRODUCTS NEEDED FOR EFFECTIVE FOREST MANAGEMENT, EVALUATE HOW THESE PRODUCTS CAN IMPROVE THE SPECIES MANAGEMENT PLAN, ASSESS CURRENT CLIMATE ADAPTATION STRATEGIES IN THE PLAN, AND PROVIDE EVIDENCE-BASED RECOMMENDATIONS TO ENHANCE CLIMATE RESILIENCE IN LODGEPOLE PINE FORESTS THAT CROSSBILLS RELY ON.ACTIVITIES TO BE PERFORMED: IN SUPPORT OF THE ANALYSES AND MODELS DESCRIBED BELOW, THE RESEARCHERS WILL CONDUCT INTENSIVE FIELD SURVEYS DURING AUTUMN IN EACH PROJECT YEAR FOLLOWING THE CASSIA CROSSBILL WORKING GROUP SURVEY PROTOCOL. FIELDWORK WILL INCLUDE STANDARDIZED POINT COUNT SURVEYS FOR CASSIA CROSSBILLS ALONG WITH CONE COUNTS AND VEGETATION ASSESSMENT AT EACH SURVEY SITE  DATA IMPORTANT FOR THE MANAGEMENT-RELEVANT DELIVERABLES DESCRIBED IN THE NEXT SECTION.DELIVERABLES AND EXPECTED OUTCOMES: THE RESEARCHERS WILL DEVELOP AND IMPROVE PRODUCTS INCLUDING A HABITAT SUITABILITY MODEL, A MICROCLIMATE MODEL, A MODEL EXAMINING MICROCLIMATE IN RELATION TO CONE PRODUCTION AND FOOD AVAILABILITY, A PREDICTIVE DISTRIBUTION MODEL FOR LODGEPOLE PINE, AND AN ANALYSIS OF POST-FIRE LODGEPOLE REGENERATION. BY CREATING THESE PRODUCTS TAILORED TO THE NEEDS OF AGENCIES RESPONSIBLE FOR HABITAT MANAGEMENT, THIS PROJECT CAN DIRECTLY INFORM STRATEGIES TO AID IN CASSIA CROSSBILL CONSERVATION.INTENDED BENEFICIARY(IES): SAWTOOTH NATIONAL FOREST, IDAHO DEPARTMENT OF FISH AND GAME, AND U.S. FISH AND WILDLIFE SERVICESUBRECIPIENT ACTIVITIES: THE UNIVERSITY OF WASHINGTON WILL SUBAWARD TO BOISE STATE UNIVERSITY TO EXECUTE THE RESEARCH OBJECTIVES OF THIS PROJECT.

PROJECT PERIOD: 9 16 24-9 15 25PROJECT TITLE: ASSESSING WILDLIFE POPULATION TRENDS ACROSS SHRUBLANDS, GRASSLAND AND ALPINE ECOSYSTEMSWILDLIFE IN GRASSLAND, SHRUBLAND AND ALPINE ECOSYSTEMS LIVE IN DYNAMIC AND CHANGING ENVIRONMENTS. THE ECOSYSTEMS AND HABITATS ARE CHANGING WITH GROWING HUMAN POPULATIONS AND ASSOCIATED CHANGES IN LAND USE AND ENVIRONMENTAL AND CLIMATIC CONDITIONS. MANY SPECIES AND POPULATIONS OF CONSERVATION CONCERN ARE RESPONDING TO CHANGES IN ENERGY DEVELOPMENT, INCREASED WILDFIRE, DISEASE SPREAD, AND SHIFTS IN CLIMATIC CONDITIONS. THESE CHANGES ARE DEPARTING FROM HISTORICAL PATTERNS, AND OCCURRING IN NEW PLACES AND AT ALTERED PACES, MAKING SPECIES CONSERVATION AND MANAGEMENT MORE DIFFICULT. FEDERAL AND STATE AGENCIES AND PARTNERS NEED TO UNDERSTAND HOW WILDLIFE RESPONSES TO ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS ARE CHANGING, TO DEVELOP NEW STRATEGIES FOR WILDLIFE CONSERVATION AND MANAGEMENT. HOWEVER, THIS CAN BE A CHALLENGING TASK REQUIRING BOTH HISTORICAL ANALYSES OF PAST PATTERNS, PROJECTION ANALYSES OF NEAR-TERM TRENDS, AND FORECASTING SIMULATIONS TO ASSESS LONG-TERM TRAJECTORIES. PROPOSE TO DEVELOP A SUITE OF WILDLIFE RESPONSE MODELS THAT ASSESS HOW SPECIES HAVE RESPONDED TO PAST, CURRENT, OR POTENTIAL FUTURE CHANGE FACTORS. COLLECTIVELY, THESE SPATIAL MODELS AND TOOLS SHOULD DIRECTLY INFORM MANAGEMENT DECISIONS TO HELP CONSERVATION POPULATIONS OF BIRDS AND UNGULATES ACROSS THESE SYSTEMS.  TO SUPPORT U.S. GEOLOGICAL SURVEY AND PARTNERS BY DEVELOPING A SUITE OF WILDLIFE ANALYSES ADDRESSING SPECIES RESPONSES TO CHANGES IN VEGETATION, DISTURBANCES FROM ENERGY DEVELOPMENT AND FIRES, DISEASE, CLIMATE CHANGE AND OTHER DISTURBANCES. WILL FOCUS ON PRIORITY SPECIES OF CONSERVATION CONCERN AND KEY CAUSES OF CHANGE WITHIN GRASSLAND, SHRUBLAND AND ALPINE ECOSYSTEMS. SPECIFICALLY, PROPOSE TO FOCUS ANALYSES ON 1) UNGULATE RESPONSES TO CHRONIC WASTING DISEASE SPREAD  2) GREATER SAGE-GROUSE AND SONGBIRD RESPONSES TO LAND-USE CHANGE IN SHRUBLANDS AND GRASSLANDS  3) AND WHITE-TAILED PTARMIGAN RESPONSES TO ALPINE CLIMATIC CHANGE. METHODS WILL GENERALLY INCLUDE THE FOLLOWING: 1) GATHERING, EVALUATING AND ANALYZING AVAILABLE VEGETATION AND WILDLIFE DATA  2) CREATING, UPDATING, OR MODIFYING SPATIAL LAYERS OR MODELS  3) ASSESSING OR QUANTIFYING RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN SPATIAL FACTORS AND ECOLOGICAL RESPONSES  4) EVALUATING LANDSCAPE, HABITAT, OR POPULATION OUTCOMES  5) SHARING AND SOLICITING FEEDBACK WITH PARTNER AGENCIES. WILL USE A RANGE OF STATISTICAL ANALYSES, CONNECTIVITY MODELS, STRATEGIC LITERATURE REVIEWS, AND GIS TOOLS TO CONDUCT THIS WORK. RESEARCH ON THESE TOPICS WILL SUPPORT THE U.S. GEOLOGICAL SURVEY, BUREAU OF LAND MANAGEMENT, AND STATE PARTNERS IN BETTER UNDERSTANDING RESOURCE NEEDS AND POPULATION CONDITIONS OF SPECIES OF CONSERVATION CONCERN ACROSS GRASSLAND, SHRUBLAND, AND ALPINE ECOSYSTEMS. THE RESULTING DATASETS, MODELS, AND TOOLS WILL SERVE AS DECISION SUPPORT RESOURCES AND CAN DIRECTLY INFORM LAND MANAGEMENT AND FEDERAL AND STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY DECISIONS ON MANAGING WILDLIFE POPULATIONS IN CHANGING ECOSYSTEMS.

PROJECT TITLE: 9 16 24-9 15 25PROJECT TITLE: UNDERSTANDING CHANGES IN VEGETATION DYNAMICS OVER TIME AND SPACEACROSS THE WESTERN U.S., SAGEBRUSH ECOSYSTEMS ARE CHANGING DUE TO A RANGE OF NATURAL AND ANTHROPOGENIC CAUSES, INCLUDING WILDFIRE AND ANNUAL GRASS INVASION BUT ALSO VEGETATION RESTORATION EFFORTS. RESTORATION OF DISTURBED SITES AND STRESSOR MANAGEMENT IS URGENTLY NEEDED IN AREAS THAT FACE CONTINUING DEGRADATION BY SEVERAL THREATS. UNDERSTANDING WHERE AND WHEN ECOSYSTEMS ARE UNDERGOING CHANGES, AND WHAT KINDS OF ACTIONS ARE SUITED TO EACH PROBLEM OR CONTEXT CAN SUPPORT TIMELY AND EFFECTIVE MANAGEMENT OF SAGEBRUSH AND GRASSLAND SYSTEMS. MANAGERS AND PRACTITIONERS HAVE FEW TOOLS THAT ARE CAPABLE OF SYSTEMATICALLY ASSESSING VEGETATION CHANGE AT MULTIPLE SPATIAL AND TEMPORAL SCALES. MULTI-SCALE TOOLS ARE NEEDED AS SAGEBRUSH AND GRASSLAND ECOSYSTEMS ARE SPATIALLY EXPANSIVE, YET VEGETATION CONSERVATION AND MANAGEMENT ACTIONS TEND TO BE PLANNED AT THE LOCAL LEVEL AND TAKE A LONG TIME TO GROW. ANALYSES AND TOOLS THAT CAN REPRESENT CHANGE AT LOCAL- AND LANDSCAPE-LEVELS, AND SHORT- AND LONG-TERM TIME HORIZONS ARE NEEDED TO UNDERSTAND THE IMPORTANCE AND INFLUENCE OF BOTH DISTURBANCES AND RESTORATION ACTIONS. TO DEVELOP MODEL-BASED TOOLS TO HELP UNDERSTAND HOW SAGEBRUSH VEGETATION DYNAMICS ARE CHANGING OVER SPACE AND TIME, BECAUSE OF DISTURBANCES, NATURAL RECOVERY, AND WITH RESTORATION EFFORTS. THESE SPATIAL TOOLS COULD DIRECTLY INFORM DECISIONS REGARDING WHERE AND WHEN TO PLANT SAGEBRUSH AND OTHER VEGETATION, HOW TO RESTORE IT EFFECTIVELY, AND HOW TO MANAGE AND TREAT INVASIVE ANNUAL GRASSES TO SUPPORT SAGE-GROUSE CONSERVATION AND POPULATION RECOVERY. SPECIFICALLY, WILL USE SPATIAL-STATISTICAL MODELING TO EVALUATE THE KEY DRIVERS AND ECOLOGICAL CONDITIONS THAT ARE ASSOCIATED WITH NEW INVASIONS AND DEVELOP MAPS OF FUTURE POTENTIAL INVASION DUE TO CLIMATE CHANGE AND LAND-USE CHANGE. TO SUPPORT MANAGEMENT AGENCIES IN IDENTIFYING THE LOCATIONS THAT MOST BENEFIT FROM CHEMICAL CONTROL OF INVASION, WILL SYNTHESIZE EXISTING INFORMATION DESCRIBING THE ECOLOGICAL CONDITIONS ASSOCIATED WITH EFFECTIVE USE OF HERBICIDES IN AREAS INVADED BY INVASIVE ANNUAL GRASSES. TO GUIDE THE PLACEMENT OF NEW RESTORATION ACTIONS, WE WILL ASSESS STRUCTURAL AND FUNCTIONAL SAGEBRUSH CONNECTIVITY ACROSS THE SAGEBRUSH BIOME TO IDENTIFY VEGETATION RESTORATION OPPORTUNITIES. THE RESULTS WILL INDICATE WHERE SAGEBRUSH-ASSOCIATED VEGETATION IS WELL CONNECTED, HAS LOST CONNECTION AND WHERE CONNECTIONS COULD BE STRENGTHENED WITH VEGETATION RESTORATION ACTIONS. WILL USE A RANGE OF STATISTICAL ANALYSES, CONNECTIVITY MODELS, STRATEGIC LITERATURE REVIEWS, AND GIS TOOLS TO CONDUCT THIS WORK. THE RESULTING SCIENCE PRODUCTS ARE EXPECTED TO SUPPORT THE U.S. GEOLOGICAL SURVEY, BUREAU OF LAND MANAGEMENT, AND STATE PARTNERS IN MONITORING AND EVALUATING VEGETATION RESTORATION NEEDS AND ACTIONS. DEVELOPING A BETTER UNDERSTANDING OF THE NATURE, DRIVERS, AND CONSEQUENCES OF VEGETATION CHANGE CAN HELP MANAGERS ANTICIPATE CONSEQUENCES OF ECOLOGICAL CHANGE, AND ACCEPT, DIRECT, OR RESIST TRANSITIONS TO ALTERNATIVE STATES. ASSESSING SPATIO-TEMPORAL CHANGES IN VEGETATION COMPONENTS SUCH AS SAGEBRUSH COVER AND INVASIVE ANNUAL GRASSES, COULD INFORM BUREAU OF LAND MANAGEMENT DECISIONS REGARDING VEGETATION CONSERVATION AND RESTORATION EFFORTS, PLACEMENT OF FUEL BREAKS AND WILDFIRE SUPPRESSION AREAS. IN LOCATIONS WITH SPECIES AT RISK OF DECLINE, VEGETATION CHANGE MODELS COULD ALSO SUPPORT HABITAT RECOVERY AND CONSERVATION PLANNING FOR FOCAL WILDLIFE SPECIES INCLUDING THE GREATER SAGE-GROUSE.

THESE WETLANDS ARE VITAL FOR WILDLIFE HABITATS AND COASTAL COMMUNITY PROTECTION, BUT THEY ALSO CONTAIN NATIVE AMERICAN CULTURAL ARTIFACTS IN SHELL MOUNDS (MIDDENS). THESE MOUNDS, CREATED BY PRE-CONTACT INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES, CONTAIN SHELLS, POTTERY FRAGMENTS, BEADWORK, AND OTHER MATERIALS. AS COASTAL LANDSCAPES CHANGED WITH RISING SEA LEVELS, MANY SURROUNDING AREAS TRANSFORMED INTO WETLANDS AND BARRIER ISLANDS. THE DISTINCT ELEVATION OF MIDDENS CREATES UNIQUE ECOLOGICAL NICHES AND ENHANCES HABITAT BIODIVERSITY.
